name: TMJ splint (orthotic)

lead: A TMJ splint is a removable acrylic appliance, usually custom-made by a dentist, that fits over the upper or lower teeth. In looksmaxxing circles the idea is that correcting jaw-joint imbalance can improve bite, jaw symmetry and facial balance.

Stabilization splints sit flat against the opposing teeth to relax the jaw muscles and spread bite forces. Repositioning splints hold the lower jaw in a different position, for example forward, to try to improve how the joint disc sits while worn. Studies focus on pain and joint function, and reviews describe modest evidence for hard stabilization splints in TMD pain and insufficient evidence on other points; appearance outcomes have not been researched.

paras: A dentist takes impressions and fits the splint, which is typically worn at night or for set periods, with follow-up adjustments. Use is generally considered reversible.

Partial-coverage splints can cause unwanted tooth movement, and orthodontic literature describes posterior open bites after repositioning splint therapy, which can need orthodontic work. Fit and use are monitored by the dentist.

angle.text: Users interested in jaw alignment discuss custom splints that stabilize or reposition the jaw joint, hoping for a more even bite and a more balanced face. Splints are used for TMJ disorders with modest evidence, and appearance outcomes have not been researched.

lead: A TMJ splint, also called an occlusal splint, bite splint or night guard, is a removable dental appliance molded to the upper or lower teeth. It is used to protect teeth, manage temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders, stabilize the joint, or alter the bite position.[1][2]

Two broad types are described. Stabilization (Michigan-type) splints sit flat against the opposing teeth to help relax jaw muscles. Repositioning splints hold the jaw in a different position, for example forward, in an attempt to improve the relationship of the joint disc.[1]

The appearance link runs through the teeth, the chewing muscles and the jaw. A splint worn at night can protect teeth from the flattening, chipping and fracture that grinding causes, which helps keep the smile and tooth shape intact; jaw-muscle overuse from bruxism can also enlarge the masseter, and people interested in jaw symmetry and bite discuss splints in that context.[3] Jaw pain, clicking and limited opening, which splints are prescribed to ease, can also affect how comfortably people chew, train and talk.[2]

Reviews summarized on Wikipedia report modest evidence of benefit for properly adjusted hard stabilization splints in TMD pain, and insufficient evidence on other points.[2] No study found tested splints for facial appearance.
infobox: Heat-cured acrylic; soft acrylic, composite or vinyl for short-term use[1]
Mostly at night; stabilization splints used for about 2 to 3 months in many protocols[2]

paras: Dental occlusal splints are acrylic and can be hard or soft, covering all the teeth of one arch or only some of them. Upper (maxillary) splints are more common than lower (mandibular) ones.[1][2] Heat-cured acrylic is the standard material and the most durable; soft acrylic, light-cured composite and vinyl are cheaper and faster to make but wear out sooner.[1]

Stabilization splints are hard, flat-surfaced appliances that position the teeth in an intended relationship to reduce abnormal muscle activity. They take more effort to make, need a face-bow record and are typically used for about two to three months.[2] Partial-coverage splints, such as one covering only the upper front teeth, can push covered teeth in and let uncovered teeth over-erupt, and some experts discourage long-term use.[2] Anterior positioning splints aim to move the disc forward and are rarely used.[2]

Soft splints suit children because growth changes the fit of hard splints.[1] A neuromuscular splint, made after low-frequency electrical stimulation (ULF-TENS) to find a jaw position, is described as a repositioning splint used diagnostically before major reconstruction.[1]

Sports mouthguards, over-the-counter 'boil and bite' guards and clear orthodontic aligners are related but separate products; this article concerns dentist-made splints for joint and bite purposes.[1]

Splints are prescribed for temporomandibular disorders and for bruxism. TMD is described as affecting about 34 percent of people globally by one estimate, usually people aged 20 to 40, more often women, and as the second most frequent cause of orofacial pain after dental pain; its three cardinal signs are jaw pain or tenderness, limited movement and joint noises such as clicking.[2] Splints are usually worn at night, so Wikipedia notes they likely do little for daytime clenching.[2]
A splint worn for bruxism mainly protects teeth from wear rather than stopping the grinding.[3]

In appearance terms, a night splint preserves the biting edges and surfaces of the teeth. Bruxism wears enamel, after which softer dentine wears faster and weakened teeth may fracture, and masseter enlargement is among its recognised signs.[3] Mouthguards and splints are also worn at night to protect thin porcelain restorations and during tooth bleaching.[1]

Bite appliances grew out of mouth protection. Boxers used cotton, tape, sponge or wood, and British dentist Woolf Krause began fitting boxers with gutta-percha mouth strips in 1892; his son Phillip is often credited with the first reusable mouthpiece, used in a 1921 fight.[1] Rodney Lilyquist, a Los Angeles dentist, introduced a transparent acrylic splint in 1947 and 1948 and is called the father of the modern mouthguard; the ADA recommended latex mouthguards for contact sports in 1960.[1]

On the jaw-joint side, the dental profession once blamed bite abnormalities for TMD, a view championed by Ramfjord in the 1960s; Wikipedia says the occlusion theory has largely fallen out of favour because bite abnormalities are very common and do not differ significantly between people with and without TMD.[2] Splints remain a widely used reversible option.[2]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: Proponents of the idea describe splints as a way to address jaw-joint imbalance that they believe may contribute to bite problems or jaw asymmetry. No published research tests this for facial appearance.

On T Nation, discussion is mostly practical. One lifter describes treating a TMJ muscle problem like a sports injury, avoiding small chewy foods and noticing grinding on waking, and considering wearing his mouthguard around the clock.[4] A 2015 post suggests TMJ problems as a possible cause of persistent sacroiliac joint pain.[5]

A review cited as 2004 found insufficient evidence for or against stabilization splints compared with other active treatments, with weak evidence that they may reduce pain compared with no treatment; a 2010 review found modest efficacy for properly adjusted hard stabilization appliances, while other types had some randomised-trial support but a higher risk of adverse events.[2] There is slightly more evidence for splints in sleep bruxism than in TMD, and excess wear on a splint can help confirm sleep bruxism.[2]

A meta-analysis cited on the occlusal splint page states there is not enough evidence that splints effectively treat sleep bruxism, with possible benefit for tooth wear.[1] Randomised trials of repositioning splints generally show no benefit over other therapies, and in a minority of cases a splint may worsen sleep bruxism.[3] A 2020 overview of systematic reviews found botulinum toxin type A in the masseter and temporalis reduced pain and sleep bruxism frequency compared with placebo or conventional treatment, with injections typically lasting about three months.[3]

Evidence comes mostly from TMD and bruxism research rather than appearance. Reviews summarized on Wikipedia report modest efficacy for hard stabilization splints against pain compared with no treatment or non-occluding appliances, and insufficient evidence compared with other active treatments.[2] A meta-analysis found not enough evidence that splints treat sleep bruxism.[1]

Smaller clinical reports include a Russian study in which TMJ repositioning and functional rehabilitation was achieved in 87.2 percent of cases with a splint plus hydraulic pressing, a minimally invasive combination.[6] Reports from a functional orthodontics practice describe splint therapy combined with open joint surgery in 60 patients (117 joints) who had not responded to earlier treatment.[7][8]
No studies found testing splints for changes in facial appearance.

Splints are generally considered reversible. Soft splints occasionally worsen TMD discomfort, partial-coverage designs can cause unwanted tooth movement, and other splint types carry a higher risk of adverse events; Wikipedia says a stabilization splint should be well fitted, used briefly and stopped if it is painful or increases pain.[2] Most sources advise against irreversible treatments for TMD.[2]

Dental literature describes a difficult orthodontic problem in patients stabilized with an anterior repositioning splint: a posterior open bite can develop, with the front teeth meeting only in the splint-stabilized position, and orthodontic treatment may be proposed afterwards.[9][10][11]

Other TMD options described on Wikipedia include jaw exercises and massage, cognitive behavioural therapy (supported by meta-analysis), medication, and botulinum toxin injection into the lateral pterygoid, which has trial evidence of benefit but can cause a fixed facial expression.[2] For bruxism, stress management, biofeedback and botulinum toxin are discussed; occlusal adjustment is regarded by many researchers as unsupported.[3]

lore.intro: Among lifters and appearance-focused communities, splints are discussed as a response to jaw clicking, grinding and perceived bite or jaw imbalance.[4][5]
